**What is asked.** The percent return of crude oil futures (Yahoo's CL=F) minus that of S&P 500 futures (ES=F), from the close on Friday 20 November to the close on Friday 4 December 2026, in percentage points.

**Starting prices.** Yahoo shows CL=F closing at $83.98 on 20 November, the last print of the expired December contract. The series now follows January, which closed at $83.41, so crude starts 0.7% behind.

**What changed since my forecast of 22 November.** Futures reopened on Sunday evening, so the window has begun. S&P 500 futures were up 1.9% to 2.1% (Bloomberg at 9:07 a.m. Tokyo on 23 November; Fortune, 22 November, 7:13 p.m. ET). January WTI was down 0.7% at $82.84 (Bloomberg) and near $83.15 later (Trading Economics, 23 November), about 1% below $83.98. The gap already stands near -3 points, so I move the centre from -0.8 to -3.0. Weekend Gulf news was hostile but did not lift oil: Iran struck Bahrain on Saturday and tanker incidents were reported around Hormuz on Sunday (ABC and Euronews, 22 November), yet prices slipped on steady Gulf exports and a forecast supply surplus (Investing.com, 22 November).

**Width.** Slightly narrower. Crude has moved about 2% a day, with bigger two-week swings ($101.47 on 27 October to $86.85 on 9 November), and the VIX ended Friday at 35.89. Over nine and a half sessions (Thanksgiving closed, a half day on 27 November) I give crude a standard deviation near 7.5 points and ES near 6, about 10 for the gap, with fat tails.

**Scheduled.** The PCE price index on 25 November, OPEC+ on 29 November to set 2027 quotas, the jobs report on 4 December.

**What would move it.** A clash over the US blockade of Iranian ports that cut Gulf flows would lift crude sharply while shares fell. A deal with Iran, a looser OPEC+ or a lasting share rebound would push the gap below -10.

**Forecast.** Median -3.0 points; middle half -9.1 to +3.1; 5th to 95th percentile -18.7 to +13.4, with nearly 2% below -25 and about 1% above +25.
